newsitem.title: USA: Oakland school board amends Ebonics plan.
newsitem.headline: Oakland school board amends Ebonics plan.

text.p: The Oakland school board, responding to a storm of criticism, voted Wednesday to alter parts of a plan that recognised black English or Ebonics as a distinct language.
After three hours of heated debate that ended just before midnight, the board unanimously approved an amended version of its December resolution that sparked national controversy.
The new resolution removed references to Ebonics as "genetically based" and as the "primary language" of many African-American students.
The board also deleted part of the resolution that -- despite the board's denials -- was widely taken to mean that it wanted African-American students to be taught in Ebonics.

The new resolution said studies had shown that African Language Systems had origins in West and Niger-Congo languages and were "not merely dialects of English." The board recognised the existence of black English and said "these are language patterns that many African-American students bring to school."
It urged school officials to draw up an academic programme to help students master English "while respecting and embracing the legitimacy and richness" of Ebonics.
Board president Jean Quan said implementing the policy would be "the real hard work."
"Wordsmithing the resolution is not going to really make that much difference," she said.
Later, she told reporters that the changes in the wording did not alter the intent of the resolution.
Ebonics, derived from "ebony" and "phonics," describes speech patterns used by some African Americans. Opinions differ as to whether it is a language, a dialect or slang.
The Oakland school district is the only one in California where black students are in the majority.
During a heated 90-minute public comment period, some speakers criticised the board for changing the resolution while others opposed it in any form.
Quan repeatedly appealed to the noisy crowd to allow people to speak and once threatened to cut short the meeting.

Robert Moody, a member of a group called Africans United for Self Help, opposed changing the original resolution, saying: "We need to stand on our own two feet ... I defy anyone of another race to tell us how to speak."
"America, you've got to wake up. You can't tell us what to do," he said.

Deborah Wright, who said she was a former candidate for Congress, attacked the board's efforts. "Your policy that attempts to legitimise poor grammar and identify it with black America will set us back 100 years," she said.
Ann Johnson, assistant principal of Franklin elementary school in Oakland, supported the amended resolution, saying Ebonics was an effective classroom tool. "It is a sound initiative," she said.
Some black leaders, local officials and the Clinton administration sharply criticised Oakland's original resolution, adopted by the board on Dec. 18.

Oakland school officials insisted all along that the policy had been misunderstood and they would not teach Ebonics in place of standard English. By recognising Ebonics, they said they hoped to improve the way black students are taught to read and write standard English.
